utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Before the witness is being brought in, I would like to raise two or three matters. The first has something to do with our decision to sit only three days and not four days a week in the month of June. The result of that is the following. The Chamber will cancel the hearings on the 7th of June. That will be a shorter hearing because of the Judges' plenary, as I told you the last time. The 14th of June, the 25th of June, and the 28th of June. And for the record, and to clarify the situation, we are sitting on the 31st of May, the 1st and 2nd of June. The 8th, 9th, and 10th of June. The 15th, 16th, and 17th of June. The 22nd, 23rd, and 24th of June. And, finally, the 29th and 30th of June, and the 1st of July. That means always three sitting days together. That is perhaps convenient enough, especially for the Prosecution and the calling of witnesses. The second matter deals with two exhibits received yesterday, P240 and P242. The Exhibit P240, we only have it in B/C/S, but this seems not to be problem because this is 5 pages from a book, entitled "Record of Sent Notes." This is in fact only a collection of numbers, and there is no need for a translation. But the exhibit P242 has no B/C/S translation, and therefore, will be only marked for identification pending translation into B/C/S. Yes, we wait a moment, there is no record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope somebody is working on it. In order to explain the situation for those watching the hearing or listening to us, there is a computer problem at the moment, and we can't continue without the computer. We hope that problem will be solved very soon. Now the problem is solved. We can continue. I have to repeat the problem of translation of exhibits. We received yesterday two exhibits. It's P240, these are 5 pages from a book, entitled "Record of Sent Notes." In fact this is only a list of numbers, and there is no need for an English translation. But the Exhibit P242 has no B/C/S translation, and therefore, will only will mark for identification pending translation into B/C/S. If there is nothing else to raise at the moment, the witness should be brought in the windows should be closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We wait a moment. For your information, the protective measures are still in place, and I would like to remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone present and the witness, and I hope that this final judgement in the whole trial comes to a conclusion in keeping with God's will. May I request that you tell me at the beginning how much time I have left, and I will adjust my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was told that you have already spent one hour and thirty minutes for your cross-examination. We will leave you time enough for continuing your cross-examination, but in the first session of this morning the Prosecution must have the possibility to re-examine the witness. So I think one hour and fifteen [sic] minutes could be enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You used one hour, thirteen minutes. There's a mistake in the transcript. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I would appreciate it if you answer some questions with just a yes or no. We need to complete this examination, and we are pressed for time because the Prosecutor needs to conduct his redirect.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, I turned off the microphone. Could you answer this question: Did your service monitor conversations of the MUP or the BH Army to establish whether there were any leaks of information through these conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On what sites were the radio-relay locations of the VRS that you intercepted and which intercepts we are seeing in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered yesterday, if you remember, that I did not have that information. I just used the resources that the 2nd Counter-Intelligence -- sorry, Counter-Electronic Protection Company had of the BH Army Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show 65 ter 2923.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that's Exhibit P239.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading only the first sentence of this document, and you can follow. I quote: "On the said day, 12th of July, 1995, monitoring the Zvornik-Vlasenica radio-relay route on frequency 785," et cetera, "we registered the following conversation:" Since the intercepts shown here concern the radio-relay route Vlasenica-Zvornik, do you know if there is any direct radio-relay route monitored by RRU 800 from Zvornik to Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said it. I was told that that was the route and that this frequency belongs to that route, and that is how I put it in my reports. And we could very frequently witness, hear ourselves, that participants in conversations were mentioning events happening on that route or along that route, so we could make the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you if there was a direct radio-relay route Zvornik-Vlasenica subject to monitoring by RRU 800.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the radio-relay devices were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this radio-relay route, on this route in general, is there optical and other visibility that makes it possible to make a radio-relay connection?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were, so I don't know. But logically, if connection was established and conversations were intercepted, it's logical to assume that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have 1D160, in Serbian page 4, paragraph 1, lines 5 and 6; and in English it's the third page, and paragraphs 3, 4, and 5. We'll have it in just a moment. This is page 1. Can we see page 4 in Serbian and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope this will not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still don't have the Serbian. Thank you, now we have it. There you see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, you said the following, I quote: "During the operation in Srebrenica, our service monitored only the frequency 8360." Is this quotation correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone. Mr. Tolimir, the microphone should be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My legal advisor says it's not the right document. In Serbian, we need the page before this one so that the witness can see what exactly he said. Could you turn to the page before in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's on the screen, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please read the last line: "During the whole Srebrenica operation, my service only monitored the frequency 836.000." Did I quote this correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's true that this was the frequency that was fully monitored, fully supervised at the time, and we monitored only that frequency. And in the event that actually occurred -- could I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No need. We will get confirmation now. Could we show the witness 65 ter 02932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would request the Court make sure that the witness is allowed to explain any answer. And, of course, if it's not an explanation, he shouldn't be allowed to do so, but as far as I believe, that it's the policy of this Trial Chamber to allow witnesses to explain their answers. And no one has rushed General Tolimir, and so this idea that he needs to rush, I think, is a false idea, and we have no problem with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think every witness should answer to the best of his knowledge and belief, and, therefore, sometimes it's necessary not just to have an answer yes or no, but an explanation. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness to confirm first whether he had, indeed, said this and to confirm. I didn't ask anything else. But if he does want to, he can first confirm and then explain, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, did you actually say what I've just quoted?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I've also tried to explain a moment ago what I said the day before; namely, that it was the priority in our work and that this frequency, with certain channels, was monitored by us continuously every day. But when, on a certain day, we established that the people we were interested in were not in their offices, were not by the phone, not wishing to waste time we scanned new frequencies or intercepted other conversations on other frequencies, which is quite normal in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you do need to, you can explain, but just look at this document. And we see that a conversation was intercepted on frequency 785; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it was not intercepted on the frequency 836?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your claim that you monitored only the frequency 836 correct, when we see that you also monitored 785 megahertz?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in order to reach the frequency 836, we had to do a lot of scanning and searching into what is being said on which frequency. Now, when we establish that a certain frequency was used by people who were of special interest to us, we assigned men to monitor these frequencies. During breaks, when these people we were interested in were not there, we continued scanning and searching. And when we came across an interesting conversation, we certainly recorded it and intercepted it. We always scanned and searched for new frequencies that might be interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please listen carefully again to what you said: "In the course of the operation in Srebrenica, our service only followed -- monitored the frequency 836." Did I quote you correctly? Only that frequency?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've tried to give you an explanation. I don't know what else I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Whilst intercepting conversations, did you leave out portions of conversations whilst transcribing them?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to cast my mind back to that time. Well, I've already said that if there were intercepts which were of no interest, we would describe them in a sentence or two. The recording would remain complete. It was only our assessment that the conversation, the substance, was not interesting, and we would only give a description of what it was roughly about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up 65 ter 2909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P243. It would be more convenient to use the exhibit number you have since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a note of it here, but I made a note of it at the moment when it was showed to the witness. So I have it as 65 ter 2909. This is the first intercept in the folder we were given, and that's how I made a note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see it? You can see that the first word in this conversation -- or, rather, the first sentence is as follows: "General Mladic is in the field, and he, too, is away." Line 2: "I can only put him through to General Gvero, if he wants." And that's what the operator at the switchboard said. I quote: "Please. "Hold on. "Hello, this is Gvero." That's Gvero speaking, and he's asking: "Who? And she says: "Svetlana," the interpreter there at Gobillard's. "My regards to you and to General Gobillard." That's what Gvero says. So Svetlana could be heard talking up until the moment you exclude the interlocutor, and you go on to transcribe only what Gvero says. Did you knowingly leave this out? Because apparently Svetlana could be heard here and you could hear her. You wrote down her name. This is something that is heard by -- you can hear the operator and what Gvero says, and you have it here, but you don't have the bits said by Svetlana. Did you leave any other portions of this conversation with General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're mistaken. I think that these were only speakers who could be heard on one end. When he said, Who, then he's the one who says Svetlana. He was told it that was Svetlana, so he just repeats her name, Svetlana. So what I believe is that we only have a transcription of the speaker speaking on one end. I'm trying to recall this, but I believe that I'm right, that these are only the speakers speaking on one channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I do understand that this is an assumption of yours. But please tell me, is it not true that you have "Svetlana" written here, and from there Gvero's words follow? So please explain to us how you account for this. Explain to the Trial Chamber. In order for us to confirm that this is the case, can we call up 65 ter 300, which is the last page of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before we do so, I would like to clarify this for the Chamber. We are listening only to one side, without hearing the other. So it says here: "Hold on." And then Gvero takes the call. He's told that it's Svetlana speaking on the other end, so he says: "Svetlana," and he then says: "My regards to you and to General Gobillard." So do you understand what I'm saying? You can only hear one side, one end of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Can we call up now 65 ter 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you mean 65 ter 3000, with three 0s?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. Perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P251. And, Mr. Tolimir, please pause until the end of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the final five lines here, which is the final part of the intercept, the number 631, where it is stated: "Svetlana." And then it says: "Greetings to you, and say hello to the general." So it can't be that Gvero would be saying both "Svetlana," and then "greetings to you." The intercept goes on to say: "There were some new developments in the field during the night. We'll be able to say with more certainty in half an hour. Have the general call in half an hour, and we'll be able to give you more reliable information." And then Svetlana says: "Okay, thank you very much and goodbye." So can you please clarify this? Why is the other interlocutor omitted here, whereas the speaker could be heard perfectly? The audibility was perfect. What Gvero was saying could clearly be heard. So can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, what we can here is solely one end of the conversation, only one side. And how is this possible? I will repeat what I said yesterday. The radio-relay communication runs along two frequencies. If the micro-telephone combination of the receiver on the side we are listening to is good and if the signal is very good, it may so happen that we would hear the other end as well. In this instant case, we obviously did not hear the speakers on the other end, and the transcription clearly relates to what the speakers on one end said only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this is the case, can you tell us, is it possible that the same conversation was recorded by UNPROFOR or NATO, and that they provided the Serbian side with it, and that it was identical to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did your intercepting service co-operate with the intercepting services of UNPROFOR, NATO, and other organisations present in the field, and did they exchange information?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. But let me take you back to a conversation that I've just recalled. I don't recall the time or the speakers, but I do recall, myself, hearing a conversation where it was said the information that was published through the media of the BH Army was definitely received from the Americans because they conveyed to them the information that they received from AWACS. Don't misunderstand me. We -- this made us laugh at the time, because our comment was along the following lines: If the other side knew that there were only two individuals involved in this work, they would find it ridiculous. So please believe me when I tell you that it wasn't us who intercepted these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please don't refer to me as having said that. I didn't say that. It's the transcript that says that. Did I say it?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It must have been someone you spoke to. Thank you. Can you tell us, now that we've -- we're dealing with this document, after the bit spoken by General Gvero - we will get back to the other parts later on - these are lines 14 and 15: "Our men said that he infiltrated himself down there in order to wreak havoc." This is speaking about Naser Oric. And let me not read the entire text. In line 24, his interlocutor says: "Well, that's true. That's risky for you." Because there's a terrorist group out in the field. Do you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to have it on my screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was quoting lines 14 and 15, and you can have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there's no English translation of this part, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an OTP document, and I don't have the English translation. I'm merely showing the document the Prosecution showed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like to hear the answer, and then Mr. McCloskey. Have you seen this portion, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get a number, what he's -- because I don't think he's talking about the B/C/S that's on the page. I think he's talking about something else. But -- because the witness just said he didn't see what he was talking about. So if he can at least give us the number of the document he's talking, maybe it will clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's clear that this is the document on the screen, but the upper part of the document which is not translated into English, if I'm not mistaken. But you should clarify that, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document, as presented by the OTP, is on the screen, and I was only reading one intercept which says: "Naser, they said, infiltrated somewhere there. He went there to fuck around."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this something that you're able to find in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is this a lawful activity on the part of Naser, to get into the VRS-controlled territory? What's your opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that I should answer the question, that I should be the one to know this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you can say yes or no. It doesn't make a difference to me.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know very well that I am not supposed to know it and that there's not a chance that I should know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm happy with your answer. Is it lawful for the VRS to oppose the sabotage group of Naser Oric's which got infiltrated into the territory and laid an ambush?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I doubt if this is an appropriate question about a legal matter. This witness is an intercept witness, and I think it's better you put questions to this witness so that you can get answers from him which helps your defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President. I didn't receive interpretation, and I have no idea what you've just said. Could you please repeat it so that the interpreters can repeat it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. I doubt if this is an appropriate question about a legal matter. The witness is an intercept witness, and I think it's better you put questions to this witness that he can answer - he is not a lawyer - so that you can get answers from him which helps your defence. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think I asked the witness to say something that I would wish him to say. It's his right to say whatever he wants to say. When I examined him yesterday, he said that he only made those intercepts that he believed were important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss with you these matters. I'm giving you guidance. I think it's not appropriate to ask this witness, as an intercept witness, about lawful action on the ground, outside his area of responsibility. Please carry on and put questions to the witness, but no debate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand. Can we again call up 65 ter 2909, which is the first document from P239 led by the Prosecution yesterday, General Gvero's intercept. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why was the content of the -- or why were the words of Gvero's interlocutor left out of this transcription, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, evidently we couldn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that UNPROFOR showed such intercepts to the sides in an open and transparent way to show them that whatever actions were taken were listened to by other sides, and he said that he would not wish to divulge what his officers had to say because this was something that his organisation forbade? Was this something that you kept in mind and adhered to in making these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were obviously conversations of generals or the top echelons of the VRS which we intercepted regardless of who their interlocutors were. It was not an instruction that we were given of this nature, and I don't know that if anything went beyond the pale, if the head of the service had the power to do anything. We, who were out in the field, did not have an instruction to the effect that we should avoid recording some conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Although your answer was long, I am happy with it. General Gvero is merely answering questions put to him here, and he is pleading for the other side to refrain from any actions. And his interlocutor, an UNPROFOR officer, says that he called in NATO and asked for their intervention. Do you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall several conversations of this nature, and I do roughly recall their tenor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote line 27 for you only: "Our enemies are not the civilians in the region, and we will protect them as far as we can." That's what General Gvero says. And from all the aspects of the application of the Geneva Conventions, I would firmly uphold what he says here, but let me ask you this: You deliberately recorded the interlocutor on the other side because he employed force against one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we heard him, we would have recorded him, and we would have transcribed what he said. We would have been far happier had such statements by generals of the Army of Republika Srpska been applied in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your comment. Can we look at the following intercept, which is on the next page, 65 ter 2909.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P244.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P244 shown, please. Thank you. It's a short conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read it, and then I'll put my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you recall what this conversation relates to?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't need to remind me what it is. I'd like to say that at that point in time, everything that was taking place in the area was of exceptional importance to us, and as you can see here, there were buses gathering, et cetera. What I would like to draw your attention to is that I did not make any sort of assessments as to what this related to and on what scale it was. There were officers who cross-referenced information and analysed it in order to put it to full use for the service. My duty was to forward this sort of information. I would not wish to comment on it now, although I believe I do know why buses were being gathered, and I believe you know too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that the fuel for the buses was provided by an UNPROFOR commander, at the intervention of the Dutch minister of defence and General Nicolai, who was in Sarajevo and who you must be familiar with, since you were into intercepting? Do you know this or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with everything. I am familiar with the events in this area. There were reports which clearly defined or specified the procurement of fuel even from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's a crime if Serbs provide fuel for the people from Potocari to be evacuated, and if UNPROFOR is involved in the procurement of fuel, this is not a crime? Is my understanding of what you're saying correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I was not referring to crime. This isn't my job. I'm talking about the accounts and the reports that we came by, and I know that there were reports based on which vehicles were being provided from Serbia and from the Drina Valley in general.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's call up 65 ter 2930, which speaks exactly to what you said right now, that vehicles were being gathered in Serbia -- or, rather, not in Serbia, in Republika Srpska. I'm sure you would have noted down something like that. 65 ter 2930.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that line 1 says: "I have --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen. This is P245. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote the first line only, to save time: "I have, at the 35th, five trailer-trucks." That's the sentence you just transcribed. So in the second part of this conversation that you intercepted, 563, they speak of fuel. Line 1 says: "What are we going to do about fuel?" And they're saying this because there is no fuel, and it needs to be transported in one day. My question is as follows: Are they looking to obtain fuel for public activity, one which UNPROFOR participated in, or, in other words, overt activity, or are they seeking to obtain it for covert activity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the fuel used for? I think these reports relate mainly to activities involving transport of population. What else was it used for, I really don't know. But this was an interesting story, from my point of view. However, whether somebody analysed this and came to different conclusions, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now look at 65 ter 2932. When we look at it, read just the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P241.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Did those buses and trucks set out?" That's the second sentence. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this conversation, is there any mention of any other military activity, apart from fuel and the gathering of buses? Read it, if you need to, and tell us. Do they speak only about evacuation? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall every intercept, but I can read through and then ... From the transcript, we can see what you are saying, that fuel was being collected for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you get any intercepts concerning evacuation involving anyone apart from the VRS; for instance, civilians who were looking for the fuel, or the military who were providing it?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were many, many conversations at that time regarding these activities, the collection of fuel and transportation vehicles. I would really need time to recall all this. I can't do it off-hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have finished with this issue. Can we now show 65 ter 2968.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting, can I give you an introduction? That's the situation we discussed a moment ago when I mentioned the infiltration of groups. Now we see a transcript showing that ambushes had been set. You can see it now, and I will quote lines 12 through 14: "Listen, those ambushes I've been setting up over there on the wide road and on the part of Glodjansko Brdo - they just called me two minutes ago - there's a large collection of Turks, three continuous kilometres long, from the school in Glodi." This is a reference to columns and to ambushes. Was this column moving announced or unannounced to those forces on the ground that had set ambushes?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are mistaken again. I'm not the kind of person who can answer that sort of question. These are just transcripts of intercepts, and that was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We could analyse more of these transcripts that are introduced through you, but we don't have time. We could go on quoting from all these transcripts of intercepts that are being introduced through you. I'm not forcing you to say whether anything lawful or unlawful is mentioned here. But since you were talking about that note-book yesterday, are these conversations recorded in that note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say, if you allow me, that as far as these events are concerned involving columns of people who are fleeing through forests and ran into ambushes and got into trouble, where some people were killed even, there have been reports, and this is one of them. That's one point. And what was that other thing you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said yesterday your note-book will be arriving here. In that note-book, are there any of the intercepts that you presented here and the Prosecution introduced through you?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that all these intercepts were recorded into that work log-book - that's what it's called - and that's how they are accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And where was that log-book when you testified in other cases? Was it in the same place as now, and why was there no access to it?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has been access to it, and I believe you saw a copy of three or four pages yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness the transcript from Popovic, 1D161, lines 18 to 24, page 46 in e-court. The page number is 6160.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will tell you what you said, responding to one Defence counsel's question. He asked you: "Can you tell us where this note-book was archived? Where is it?" That was the question by Defence counsel. And you answered: "I am not authorised to say. I explained that the part of this note-book that was in the possession of my service has been copied by the Tribunal -- by the OTP. In this case, I can really not answer this question." Would you confirm, first of all, that you've said this when testifying in the Popovic case? If you say, No, then I will have no questions.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to explain? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, what is the difference between then and now concerning this note-book where intercepts were recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of my work in the service, I occupied different positions. I occupied one position at a time, which I lost later and was replaced by someone else. This log-book came to a different jurisdiction, and I no longer had access to it in a certain period, and I don't think that even now we can provide the complete log-book, because we wouldn't do something that runs counter to the interests of my service. But I can tell you, for instance, the number of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need that. The Trial Chamber and the Tribunal can ask for it, if they want to, because you say you have all of these reports. Just tell me, to the best of your knowledge, did the OTP get insight and access to all these archives of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say yes or no with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have they been given anything out of all this material and all these note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. At a certain stage, I personally made a list of all the material that had been turned over, the material that I was told to hand over and get a receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this material shared with anyone else; for instance, the Defence team here in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me for anything. Everything that was requested is accessible to the Prosecution and probably, by the same token, to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have an exchange of information of the material that, as you said, you gave to the Prosecution and that is otherwise treated as military secret?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention military secret. Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because you said you don't know and that the OTP was given only a part of this material, I'm asking whether material of this sort has been given to any other service or any other user as part of an exchange of information?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, or, rather, not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, tell me why you and the other interceptors signed off with initials that do not reflect your name, and every report you made was marked "state secret." And why is everything decrypted in the material, apart from your code-names?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was an answer, but it was not interpreted. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this particular case, I think it's -- Your Honour, I would object to this three-part question. To try to get the witness to remember all three parts is too much, in my view. If he could break it down, I have no objection to it, but he doesn't -- he's not able to read the transcript to be able to go through and figure them all out. And he's trying hard, I think you see that, but even yesterday we know that he -- and the problem with this is we don't know -- if he doesn't answer all through, we don't know which of the three questions his answer applies to, and it's really hard to try to sort that out on redirect a day or several hours later. But ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will break it down into three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were your names, as interceptors, encrypted in the telegrams sent to the Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me first ask all of the questions, and then you will clarify. Were these telegrams marked "state secret"?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we marked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In these reports, everything was decrypted and open, except the names of the interceptors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you write a report, you write it in the form as you can see it now, and then it is encrypted in its entirety, and then it is sent to the centre through communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This information we are presented with in this note-book introduced through you, is it decrypted or encrypted?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obviously decrypted. If it were encrypted, we wouldn't be able to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it necessary for the Tribunal to know what you, as an interceptor, wrote about anyone, such as the chief of your service? Why is it important to know their names?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we are moving into a completely different area that has to do with communication control and protection of data in our service. And if you want to discuss it, perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No need. I won't ask you anything about that anymore. If the Trial Chamber is interested, they will put other questions to you. You just answer this for me: In a decrypted conversation, in a decrypted intercept, do the names of the interceptors remain encrypted? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained to you, when you write on the computer the whole report and the signature of the author, this file, in its entirety, is encrypted, and then it goes through the media to the communications centre, where it comes out in the original form, where the name of the operator is again protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have here 12 intercepts that you transcribed, and there's nothing encrypted in them except your signature, which consists of initials and numbers that do not reflect your name. "JD073" is the name of your co-worker, and your signature is "JN160." Was it done at the suggestion of the OTP, or did you know back in 1995 that you would need it for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did not expect such questions from you. These are code-names of our operators used in all documents. Anything that I ever wrote in my service, I would sign as "JN160." That was my name and surname at the time in my service whenever I signed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, but this document is used in court, and you are appearing in court as a witness. Is it really necessary that your code-name remains the only protected piece of information, whereas everything else is decrypted?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, we were not working for the purposes of a court. It was standard practice, standard procedure in our service, and I'm sure you know this very well, that not a single employee of our service would sign anything with their full name. They would use the code-name. And it works the same in all such services in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, did you receive any training from anyone, apart from the members of your army, before the war or during the war? Did you travel anywhere for training that would enable you to engage in these activities during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I wouldn't like to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it have any relevance for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's relevant because it concerns my education, my approach, the methods we used in monitoring these communications, intercepting them, and the methods of conveying information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answers, for sharing your views and comments. I'm very grateful to you for helping us and the Trial Chamber understand your work. I have no further questions. I wish you a safe journey home. I have concluded my cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. And could we bring up 65 ter 1680, P240.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you'll see, when this comes up that it should be the first page, yes, of your -- of all the number in the note-book, this is one of five pages. And this is a page of the note-book we have been talking about and that General Tolimir has been talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he asked you questions about whether or not the intercepts were in the full note-book, and you said they were, and that this note-book, hopefully, is coming. Can you clarify for us, when you said the intercepts were in this note-book, are you referring to the intercepts as they are identified by number and such, as we see them on this page, or are you suggesting or saying that the entire intercepts are in this note-book as well, the text of the intercepts? Just so we can clarify that. It's a little unclear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This log-book contains transcripts -- or, rather, a reference to the numbers of the transcripts. For instance, transcript 510 at the top was logged into this book, as written here. It's the number assigned by the computer during encryption and the time when this report was sent. It's not the text of the intercepts. It's just the protocol number, a record, a register of the numbers of transcripts, and this log-book contains all the information that was transcribed at this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are there frequencies in this log-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that this concludes your examination. The Chamber would like to thank you that you came to The Hague again and to help us to consider the whole case. Thank you very much again. We will have our first break now and resume five minutes before half past 12.00. That means 12.25. The Court Officer will assist you after the Chamber has left the courtroom. Thank you very much again. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye. It's already afternoon now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. President, I did want to bring one issue to your attention. There is a document that I had intended to use with this witness. We have assigned it a provisional 65 ter number, and I've spoken to Mr. Gajic concerning it. It is a series of intercept reports that I wanted to use with this witness for only illustrative purposes, not as substantive evidence, just to familiarise the Court with how the intercepts are processed during the course of the operations. There is an intercept that is the subject of the first of these -- there are 19 reports for a series of -- on one day, on the 15th of July, 1995. The first of these intercepts is actually on the 65 ter list, and there are some other ones as well within those reports that are on the 65 ter list, but the whole of the reports, 1 through 19, is not, in and of itself, on the 65 ter list. I've spoken with Mr. Gajic to see if there would be any objection to using it with the witness for non-substantive purposes, and it appears that there isn't an objection, so I would like to ask permission of the Trial Chamber -- leave of the Trial Chamber to use this document, in other words, to add it to the 65 ter list. I know that we normally submit these applications in writing, and I think that's the best way to do it, but I think given the fact that it's uncontested, it might be more efficient to do it this way. In any event, if not, I can use only the intercept that is on the 65 ter list, of which I've given Mr. Gajic notice in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you intend to tender these additional intercept transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I don't need to tender them. I can just show them to the witness so that he can illustrate for the Court how the process works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I realise that the accused is not objecting, and leave is granted, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He is, and we're prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I think the screens should be opened first. Please be patient for a moment. Good afternoon, sir, again. Would you please read aloud the affirmation to tell the truth on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and please sit down. There are, as you know, protective measures in place for you, and Mr. Vanderpuye has some questions for you. Both parties should be reminded to switch off the microphone during the answer of the witness. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, again, good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, I'd like to show you 65 ter 6279.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, if you could take a look at the name on this exhibit, and just confirm that you are the person named in it, without telling us your name.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P253, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd just like to get a little bit of background information, if I could, from you, Witness. Mr. President, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you if there was a difference between radio communications at the 2-metre or 80-centimetre range and those of radio-relay links. If you could just briefly illustrate that for us.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Normally, there would be a difference in terms of its technical setup. But as for the link itself, the communication line is the same. The specificity of radio relay links lies in the fact that the communication runs along directional antennae, in the fact that they are used for traffic mostly of the higher-level units, from the brigade up to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was your unit able to or did your unit engage in the interception of civilian telephone lines, for example, or data lines?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: While I was its commander, our unit never monitored civilian lines. It did happen, however, that civilians would use military lines of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the three facilities you were involved with, was there a distinction between the types of communications that were intercepted among them?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: As I've already said, from the northern facility and the southern facility, radio-relay links were monitored, and partly ultra-shortwave

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear. From -- between 0 to 5, 6, 8, or 10 megahertz for these ultra-shortwave communications, visibility is not required. Since these waves do have these qualities of refraction, and these are technical terms - it doesn't really matter - but they can bend around obstacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, one location was mentioned. This page 37, line 7. Is there any problem with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just bear with me. I'm trying to locate it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 37, line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, there's a problem. Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will redact that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, was there any distinction among these facilities? And we'll try to avoid mentioning their names, but is the distinction between them in terms of the targets of the interception, that is, the facilities and objects of the operation?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: There is a distinction, and at first glance it is very simple. All radio-relay stations need to be placed on elevations high up in order for them to be able to establish communication, and there has to be optical visibility. From the military perspective, and I've already said this, the facilities in the north and in the south were part of the communications system of the Yugoslav Army, and they stayed in the territory of the BH Army. From the military perspective, we had ideal locations for monitoring radio-relay communications, even more than ideal, as it were, because we were swamped by them from all sides. The question was not whether one could monitor communications; rather, how much could be followed with the modest amateur equipment we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to know, though, is: Is there any difference between who you were -- your unit was intercepting, as among the three facilities that you were attached to? In other words, was one unit monitoring one category of people or facilities, versus another unit, or were they all monitoring the same target?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Every unit or part thereof had its respective area for radio reconnaissance. Thus, the unit in the north, for the most part, monitored the communications of the East Bosnian Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, and elements of the Drina Corps, whereas the unit in the south monitored radio-relay communications of the VRS General Staff, the Drina Corps, and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did any of the three facilities monitor, for example, political entities or political people, as distinguished from military facilities and military people?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: We were never charged with the task of monitoring political leaders. However, in performing our -- in performing their duties, political leaders used military communication systems, especially when communicating with Banja Luka, since the political authorities were at Pale, and with Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the northern and southern facilities, I wonder if you could just familiarise the Trial Chamber with how these particular facilities were set up. That is, if we could begin, perhaps, with the command structure, how it was organised in terms of personnel.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: It all depended on the amount of equipment that was available at a given point in time. Since our unit was providing support to intelligence structures and, to that end, gathered information, it was never manned 100 per cent. On average, in the northern facility the tasks were performed by a platoon of approximately 15 men. They worked according to the following system: They would spend seven days in the facility and then seven days at home. It could change depending on the frequency of traffic, so they could spend 10 or more days in the facility, and this mostly happened in the summer of 1995, and then the subsequent 10 days at home. The workload was enormous. One worked 'round the clock, under very difficult conditions, with poor equipment and poor training -- or, rather, poor clothing, I meant. And this was especially the case in the winter. There was no heating. Old heating stoves were used, if only just to keep the equipment in working order. A similar situation prevailed in the southern facility as well. This facility was even more difficult to access, especially in the winter. It was also manned by a platoon which monitored radio-relay communications with approximately 12 to 18 men; on average, 15. They had the same work regimen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the number of men that were working at each of these facilities, were they -- you said they were organised in platoons. Were they further -- were they further divided into shifts, squads, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I've already said that the work was done seven days in a stint, followed by seven days of rests. So people were divided into shifts. Half of them were resting, half of them were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many hours was a shift, for example?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the personnel, that is, the operators themselves, was there any formal training that was provided to them either prospectively, before they were recruited, or after they were recruited into your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: In order to explain that, I have to go back to 1992. The unit, as such, was established -- founded from a number of enthusiasts, mainly radio amateurs and officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, or, rather, former JNA officers who at that time were serving as officers in the BH Army. They started with modest equipment, and the unit grew to its full size in mid-1995, numbering, on average, 50 to 60. There was no professional-quality equipment either imported or inherited from the JNA. We just adapted and souped-up devices we had in our radio clubs, adding amplifiers, pre-amplifiers, and other components, and we managed to enable these devices eventually to monitor one channel from one site. Our capacities were modest, but they were used to the full. We had in our unit former JNA officers specialised in communications, and the core of the unit was made up by Ham radio operators with 10 to 40 years' experience. They were the moving force of the unit, especially when we had to deal with technical problems. There was no special training, as such, because there was too much to do. There was just training on the job, for the very simple reason that at that time we couldn't do any different. We fought to the best of our ability, and I believe we won our victory deservedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the experienced radio amateurs that worked in the unit, do you know whether or not any of them held any certification, Ham radio or amateur certifications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: All the people we had, had certificates of a completed course in radio amateurism and awards from various competitions, and they had constant shortwave communication with all continents; Europe, America, Australia. They connected to their radios, tape-recorders, and any other devices needed to establish connection. Radio amateurs have to learn the same things as radio operators. You need to be able to receive and transmit messages. But in our unit, all they had to do was to receive a message and transform it into written information. They had enormous experience, and they proved to be even better than some schooled soldiers from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of the former JNA officers that you had working in the unit, did they also have certain certifications from the former JNA in terms of communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Right this minute, I can't tell you about each individual person, but I know that we had two officers who had graduated from the military academy specialising in counter-intelligence protection and electronic warfare. But there were also officers who had graduated from the military academy in Zagreb who used to be in the air force, working on radars and communication systems of the air force, and they were a considerable reinforcement to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned a little bit about the work process, itself, but I'd like to get into a little bit more in depth of detail about what the intercept operators did in performing their functions. But if you could just describe basically how the process went in terms of receiving communications and then translating those or transcribing those into written documents.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I just want to mention something I'd forgotten to say before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I will repeat my question, just so that --

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: There's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: The process of gathering information at our work-place ran as follows: The first and primary task was to record and note down all the signals that appeared within the range to eliminate channels of no interest, mainly within the range of the RRU 800, television channels. And then once a working frequency is discovered where communication runs between two hubs of communication, or a radio station, on the one hand, and a radio-relay station, on the other hand, we would adjust our antennas to get the best signal possible, and then we would proceed to identify active channels. Our technical capacities enabled us to monitor one channel from one work-place. I know very well what the ideal situation would be and what was possible in the former JNA, but with our technical capacities, that's the only thing we could do. After we identified -- or, rather, discovered participants in the traffic, we would proceed to record the communication. People could not memorise and then note down what they heard, so they first had to make a recording, then play it back and listen, and note it down. Such information was written down into station log-books according to the recipe of the former JNA or in our working note-books, because we did not have any dedicated documents for writing this down. After a particular communication was transcribed by hand, we would type it on a computer. Once it was typed up, these reports would be encrypted and sent to the competent command. That would describe the process of work of one listener on one device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've mentioned a few machines that are involved in this process. The first is that you mentioned an RRU 800, and if you could just briefly explain that to the Trial Chamber. I believe there's been some evidence concerning what that is, so if you could be brief, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Radio-relay device RRU 800 is a classic device of the former JNA used to maintain communication at the level of higher-ranking units. It is manufactured by Siemens of Germany, and its working life is over 60 years, at least was in the former JNA. It is an analogue device. In other words, you can listen to it. It is mainly installed in stationary facilities on high mountains, and it can establish communication within a range of 50 to 80 kilometres from one hill to another. It can also communicate on longer distances, but the manufacturer gives a guarantee for up to 80 kilometres. It's mainly used for communication from the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade to what was then called army districts. It's a high-maintenance device that uses a lot of power, but the former JNA also had mobile devices, which means they could be installed, with all the supporting equipment, on a truck. They are rarely moved. They are mainly stationary, in installations where they had a constant power supply, but also a back-up power supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were the southern and northern facilities also monitoring -- sorry, I see Mr. Tolimir wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I could not hear the question interpreted, the question by Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat your question, and we will find out if this will be recorded and interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I was asking is: Were the southern and northern facilities also monitoring other radio-relay devices, such as RRU 1? And if you could explain to the Trial Chamber what that is.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: From the northern and southern facilities, apart from the RRU 800 device, which is a classic for the former JNA, whose range is 690 to 950 megahertz. There was also a device, SMC, that we couldn't monitor because that device worked on satellite frequencies, several gigahertz. It's a massive one. It's mainly connected with the supporting equipment and communicates over 120 channels. And there was also VZ 120 device. Apart from these devices, the VRS also had HVT 1 devices that operated between 400 and 500 megahertz, and the latest devices produced in Yugoslavia, RIU 1. I'll try to explain the main features of this device. It works in the range of 230 to 270 megahertz. It's very light. You can carry it on your back. It's mainly used in certain combat activities because it's easy to remove when changing position. That means that one person can carry it on their back and install it and re-install it. It uses normally two antennas, one of them directional, and it also uses a stick antenna that has a circular beam. It was very easy to discover and monitor. As I've already said, the Army of Republika Srpska used this device to set up a forward command post, to set up a tactical group, because it was rapid in connecting to RRU 800. It was easy to take it down to the telephone switchboard. You can easily plug an extension into it. For instance, when someone is calling Vlasenica, they dial three digits and that telephone will ring in Pribicevac. These are the main features.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that these communications had to be recorded, and can you tell us basically what kind of tape they recording on and what kind of machine was used to accomplish this?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: That was our second-greatest problem, where to record this huge amount of information, how to keep it, and on what to record it. All these communications, voice communications, were recorded throughout the war onto traditional reporter recorders that were formerly used by journalists. They were called UHER. We got them from radio stations such as Radio Tuzla, from major companies where they had been used to record meetings of the workers council before the war, and we also got all the tapes. We didn't have any new tapes. We didn't have food, let alone tapes. We also got them from radio stations such as Tuzla, Banovici, Gradacac, and such, and we recorded onto those tapes. After the content was typed up, we would dub more important communications onto a different tape, and we would erase the original tapes and put them back into use.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have in e-court, please, 65 ter 1639.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see the machine that's on the screen in front of you, Mr. Witness? Could you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: This is the traditional UHER recorder, manufactured in Germany, that we used in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could just go to the next page, please. I'm sorry, it's 1640, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You recognise this machine as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes. That's a type of recorder we used in our work. Let me say that this type of recorder was used by the listening units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I have one other I would like to show you, and I understand it is 1641.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: That's also a type of recorder, UHER recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are these three types that I've shown you the types that were used by your unit in at least 1995, if not for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes, these recorders were used in 1995 and before 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender all three of these photographs. The first is 1639.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P254.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The next is 1640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, this one as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P255.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the last is 1641.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P256.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, in the process of interception as it occurred in these facilities, northern and southern, were the operators provided with any additional information concerning the areas that they were monitoring or the events that they were monitoring?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I've already said that intelligence gathering is a painstaking process. It is only normal that as the unit developed, some amount of organising and re-organising was required. All these units and parts thereof were assigned their respective zones for radio reconnaissance. This did not rule out the possibility that they would be monitoring the communications normally falling under the remit of the other unit, that's to say the northern facility, that of the southern, and vice versa. It all depended on the density of traffic. If there were certain activities taking part in the south and they could be followed from the north, it was only natural for that other unit to get involved and assist the other, and this was solely because of the modest resources we had. All these activities were regulated in an order for radio reconnaissance received from the command of the corps and were further regulated by own orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so was it the case that the intercept operators at the northern and southern sites were told or directed as to which frequencies or channels to monitor in any given situation?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: It was standard procedure. Of course, directions were received as to which links were more important and others were not. Let me note that operators, be it in the north or in the south, never knew what their colleagues in other facilities were monitoring. It so happened on many occasions that the same line would be monitored from both the northern and southern facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that the operators would at some point play back the tape and listen to it. Did they do that individually, did they do that collectively? If you could tell us a little bit about that process.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: All the play-backs of information as it arrived had the purpose of being listened to and transcribed. This would be normally done by a single person. However, in most cases where the other interlocutor could not be heard well or when weather conditions were bad, and since the frequency was not everywhere the same, one had to rely on the help of his colleagues to find out what was actually said. This was a normal process. Since the return signal sometimes was of good quality, at other times it was of poor quality, and since in some cases both could be heard on the same channel, only once everybody agreed that, indeed, a specific word was uttered would it actually be transcribed onto a piece of paper. Likewise, in view of the technical features of the UHER reel-to-reel tape-recorder, the speed would be slowed down, and the words could then be heard better. Another possibility afforded by the UHER device was that noise -- background noise could be eliminated to a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of listening to and transcribing these tapes, was that something that was done immediately after a recording was made, or is that something that was done later in the day? Was there any specific protocol concerning when and how that transcription took place?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: The transmission of information gathered primarily depended on the following factors: Number 1, the weight or importance of the information concerned. If the nature of the information dictated its urgent transmission -- let me explain it the following way. We had a map of targets in the Command of the 2nd Corps, and when artillery would open fire from Mount Ozren and open fire on Tuzla, this sort of information would not be even put on paper. You would immediately inform the municipal early-warning system and the HQ for an alarm to be sounded, because military installations were never targeted. No important targets were fired upon. Rather, indiscriminate fire was opened on the residential areas populated by the civilian population. So this is the sort of information that dictated urgency, and they would be transmitted instantly. Other sort of information, like most of the intercepts, which carried long-term importance and meant that nothing would change for the moment, would be typed up as soon as they were recorded; at most, an hour or two later. The information would be transcribed, typed up, and forwarded. One needs to bear in mind that this is a difficult, labour-intensive process, transcription, typing up, et cetera, so there was normally a lapse of one to two hours before it was completed. So sometimes we would have 35 or 30 such batches of information, sometimes 15 only, but whatever was recorded would be forwarded not soon thereafter. It happened occasionally that if we had intelligence intercepted before midnight, it would be sent at 1.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could show the witness, please, 65 ter 6283, 6283.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to show you -- this shouldn't be broadcast, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
