utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, I want to show you this document. It indicates that it is from the 2nd Corps in the title. I'm afraid there's not an English translation, just so you're aware, Your Honours, but I think we can get through it. It indicates the site, as you can see in the third line on the left. And then it has a strictly confidential number. It's "Str.pov.br. 01/15795. Do you see that, Witness? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Answer the question for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you can just -- you have to answer out loud. Do you see what I was just reading into the record?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now in terms of the number "01/15795," can you tell us what that indicates? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: This is the conventional letterhead normally used for reports from northern and southern facilities. These reports were sent to the intelligence organ of the 2nd Corps. It's a daily report of radio reconnaissance. In the left-hand corner, we have this conventional heading. Since our unit was under the 2nd Corps, (redacted) (redacted) northern facility, and this means that the intercept that follows was made in the northern facility. Then we have what is short for "strictly confidential number 01/15795." Well, this is the normal reference number assigned to this report, which consists of the following: The first number, 01, tells us that this is the first report to have been typed up and sent to the command on the 15th of July. What follows after "01" is the date, "15," the 15th, "7," July, "95," the year 1995, and this date is written below. So this is the typical report -- the typical example of a report, that is, which doesn't -- this is a typical example of a report which does not have an instantaneous importance. It was recorded on an RRU 1, and we can see below the dotted line the frequency on which it was done, 254.300 megahertz, at 2221 [as interpreted] hours, that is. Every one of these reports needs to contain an encryption indicating when exactly it was sent. This report was sent on the following day, right after midnight, and it was recorded an hour and 20 minutes before midnight. Moreover, the report indicates the interlocutors, X, a Malinich and a Nastich. What does this mean? This means that one of the participants in the conversation was Major Malinich. He introduced himself at the start. Any participant in a conversation who is not introduced, who is not known, is designated with an X or a Y. We can see it is clearly indicated when Major Malinich is speaking, or when the unknown participant is speaking, or when Nastich is speaking. So this is the typical template that was used for reports that were sent to the Command of the 2nd Corps on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt this explanation. I waited. Now we have to redact line 11 of page 52 on the right screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a different pagination, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I know that. In LiveNote, it's another page and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Also in the transcript, I'm not sure which line it is, but it's indicated the timing of this intercept is 2221. In fact -- oh, I can see it now. It's page 53, line 14. Okay. It should be 2241 is the time of the intercept, as we can all see in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, if we could just page forward to ERN 348, so it should be three pages -- or the third page, rather, in e-court. Page 4, that's it. All right. In this document, it has the same heading as the first one, but we can see, for the strictly confidential number, it starts with "02/15795." And if you'll note with respect to the first intercepted communication between X and Y, it shows a time of "0554 hours." Now, between the two, that is, the prior intercept of 2241 hours and this one that we see now at 0554 hours, can you tell us when this intercept would have been recorded and sent?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: This intercept was made at the same facility, and which, according to the reference number, was the second report on the 15th of July, 1995. The difference between this report and the earlier one is that the instant report contains information intercepted by an RRU 800. We can see that the time indicates early-morning hours. What else is typical? Well, the fact that the participants in the conversation did not introduce themselves or reveal their identity in any way. They are denoted as X/Y, meaning unknown, unidentified. What else is telling about this report? Well, the fact that at a different time, at 0611 hours, the report -- or, rather, the intercept was made on channel 784.700, on channel 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would this intercept have been recorded on the 15th of July, as opposed -- would this intercept have been recorded on the 15th of July, as opposed to the one at 2241?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: This intercept was recorded in the early-morning hours of the 15th of July, and this tells us that from 2241 hours, which is the time indicated earlier, up to this point, there was no traffic. Normally, things quietened down around midnight. So it was the second report that was sent from the northern facility to the Command of the 2nd Corps on the 15th of July. Let me also add that communications operators worked 'round the clock. They had their sleeping quarters in the office, so they were working and always available both in the corps command and in these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, is there any fixed number of reports that are required to be sent in a given date or -- on a given day, or is that a flexible system?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: The report in this particular format would be typed up at the KZ station or the encryption station. This station had a set -- special code set aside for each day. So the report would be encrypted, and only an encrypted report could be sent on the day. It would be entered in the log-book of outgoing telegrams, and then in the corps command they would have a log-book of incoming telegrams. So every day for the period of consecutive three years, the communications officers dealing with encryption would check if the number of telegrams sent out from the facility on a given day matched with the number of telegrams received in the corps command on the day. This was a standard procedure. Now, the codes for encryption were received on a monthly basis from the Main Staff in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the number of reports that are sent out, we see here in these two examples, 01, 02, is that -- is the number of these reports fixed? Are 10 reports required to be sent out on a given day, 20, 1, 2?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The number of reports depended on the activity on the other side. I've already said that there were days when 30, 40, 50 reports would be sent out, and there were days when only 2 would be sent out. The number was never fixed. Only the midnight report was fixed, because there you would check if the number of the telegrams sent out matched the number of those received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, when the operators wrote down or would write down what was on a given tape, was there any analysis that was involved in this that they were required, or authorised, I should say, to perform?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: As in every other job, some sort of analysis was conducted at all times. The primary task of operators was to record a given activity or a given conversation and transcribe it just the way it was recorded. Of course, we had note-books where we would write down specific frequencies. Let me just say that it was very easy to uncover radio-relay routes, for the simple reason that they tended to change very rarely. During my stay there, frequencies changed maybe on four -- three to four occasions, as did the names of these radio-relay stations or the names of the various participants, members of staffs or brigades. So we had the supporting documentation which facilitated and directed our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was this information provided to intercept operators, such as the names of facilities, of participants, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Naturally, every operator had to have an idea of what was happening in the field. They knew these things by heart. It wasn't a problem. The reports were analysed in detail in the Analysis Department, and based on their analysis, guide-lines were given for work. But, of course, every operator had to have an idea of how radio-relay systems in the VRS worked. So the process can at once appear simple and complicated. We would simply open up the radio-relay systems -- the empty charts of radio-relay systems used by the JNA formerly and fill them out in order to create a picture of the participants in the communication; brigades, staffs, commanding officers, the charts of wire and wireless communications, and communications systems that were in place. So this was the sort of analysis that was conducted within the unit, but the overall analysis was carried out by the Analysis Department of the 2nd Corps and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat where else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think your answer is only recorded up until you mentioned the Analysis Department of the 2nd Corps, but you also mentioned some other facilities. Could you please just repeat that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: So primary analysis was made by our unit. Because of the frequency of traffic, we didn't have time for anything else. In the Command of the 2nd Corps, there existed an analysis department, and opposite that department there existed a department for counter-intelligence protection, which had the task of analysing all the information gathered through electronic reconnaissance and to fill out all the gaps in the communications system as it existed on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think it's time for the break, and this is a good point to stop, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we break, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Thank you, Witness. On page 56 of the LiveNote, you stated that the system, as it worked, was such that all the operators, normally speaking, were warned -- were informed of the way the system operated in the VRS, all the more so since many operators had trained -- had done their training in the JNA. Now, here's my question: If such was the case, normally speaking, all the VRS operators should have known the system that operated in the ABiH, and vice versa, so everybody knew that they were being tapped; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right. Let me just make a few points. Our advantage during the war was primarily the fact that we did not have the equipment of the sort, we didn't have anything to work with. In a number of reports, you can find constant cautions from lower-level ranks to the higher-level ranks that they should be wary of what they say because these links or these routes were being monitored, so it was a cat-and-mouse game. We were the mouse, a cornered mouse, and they did not much pay attention or give importance to the fact that we listened to them. I don't know if you understand me. If you have a side that has an upper hand, then it doesn't really matter. They believe that things were going to end in their favour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, you've already answered the question I was about to ask you now. I wanted to know how it came that they were so naive. When you look at the contents of the intercepts, why were they being so frank, provided these are authentic intercepts? I was curious as to the frankness of the messages we've seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now another question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Mine is just a clarification. At page 34, lines 10 to 13, you stated that: "The main duty of any commanding officer is to assemble men and equipment to ensure that the process of gathering intelligence through electronic reconnaissance is going on smoothly and to provide necessary resources for his men." My question: Is your reference to "men" in that paragraph -- does your reference to "men" in that paragraph include women, or you had no women under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to a specific period, I can tell you that we did have women who performed other types of work. If we're talking specifically about 1995, there were no women in our ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we must have our second break, and we will resume at 2.35. The Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer [sic], please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I misspoke, Mr. Vanderpuye. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like to ask you, Witness, is I'd like to go over, I think in a little bit more detail, the process of transcribing these taped intercepted communications into note-books, and how that was done, specifically. Now, was it the case that operators always transcribed taped intercepts into note-books, in particular?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I've already said the process ran as follows: Upon detecting a conversation, in other words, the channel where the speakers were speaking, we started recording on tape-recorders. The next step would be to transcribe the communication by playing back the tape. And considering that we never had original documents, we transcribed these intercepts wherever; in paper -- on paper from old books, old forms, and note-books. We would note down every conversation in a note-book, indicating speakers, the time, the frequency. And then we would go to the KZ station, which is the encryption station, and that is where these transcripts would be typed up on a computer. According to our procedure, the report would be in its proper format once the typewritten text from a computer is printed out. Once it was typed up on a computer, it would be encrypted and sent to the relevant command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How important was it for the operators to note down the information on the tapes accurately?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: That was the most important duty of every operator. We never insisted, in our service, on how much should be written or that the operator should listen carefully to who is speaking and what they are saying. The most important task was to write down correctly in the note-book whatever was recorded on tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before you continue, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want a clarification. Page 60, line 9 to 21, you have given us a description of how the listening was done, the evidence was noted down, up to the time when it was sent to the relevant command. How many people would have been involved in this process? Is it the same person who listens, transcribes the notes, types the report, and sends it to the command, or were there other people involved in the process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The process of gathering information would involve several people, that is, from the moment of recording until the moment of play-back. We would have four to six work posts, meaning that four to six people would be present on every shift. Only one person would be doing the re-typing and encryption. That man worked in a separate room. He was the only one who had the codes for encryption. He had to have special training, and he was the only one authorised to receive and send telegrams. The person who took down the message could be present in the room only to dictate. As for play-back of tapes, if there were any indistinct passages, everyone would gather and listen carefully and give their input on what they think they were hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the note-books that the operators used to transcribe this information, who supplied these note-books to them?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I shall only say that during the whole war, at any time all of my men and I knew very well what we needed, what we wanted to have, what would be ideal, but it was wartime. We didn't have enough to eat, and note-books were unthinkable. They only started to appear on the market in 1995. We had to make due with what we had. In the summer, when there were mushrooms, we ate mushrooms. If we had some flour left over, we would swap it for note-books. We would ask friends to give us old forms to fill in. They were in the form of note-books, and you could write on the back because the back of every page was blank. Logistics were poor. We simply didn't get around to note-books because we ran short of many more important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could have in e-court, please, 65 ter 869.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while that's coming up on the screen, let me ask you this: Was there specific information that the operators were required to record in the note-books when they took down an intercept, such as the frequency or the participants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, will there be a problem if this note-book will -- this document will be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: What you see is the cover of a note-book which I think we had in 1995, and we used it to write down intercepts in it. Basically, these are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you should switch off. Witness, you should continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came to the unit, one of my priorities was to make the unit more soldierly, and we started with what we could get hold of. All these note-books, before being put to use, were registered in a record. They would get a number, a date, and be marked "Strictly Confidential," and they would be sent to the northern or the southern location. Since there were no columns printed in these note-books for various rubrics, date, frequency, intercept, et cetera, et cetera, everyone had to write and draw these lines themselves, the time and hour of the conversation, the name of the speakers if they introduced themselves, if their identity was known, or perhaps X/Y if we didn't know who they were. And then at the end of every intercept, it was the duty of the operator to put down -- to note down his own initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have an original note-book. I don't know if the Court would like to see it. I would like for the Court to see it, and I think the accused has had an opportunity to inspect it as well. But for the moment, I'd like to show it to the witness and have him explain it, some of the content. So if I could have this shown to the witness and placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is note-book 103 that's actually indicated in the exhibit -- the photographic exhibit in front of the Court now. It's on the far right in that photograph, the second one down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this whole note-book in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't believe the whole note-book is in e-court, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That could create a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to tender the note-book. I just want the witness to indicate to the Court what he's talking about, in terms of the notations that are in it. But for the purposes of e-court, I'm going to tender just the photographs of it, because there are other documents that establish the connection, without tendering the physical exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you indicate -- is the ELMO functioning? I'd like the witness just to show the Court the strictly confidential number that you've indicated were written down in these note-books. If we could just place that on the ELMO so we can see where those are marked -- that number's indicated, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, if you could just indicate to the Court where the "Strictly Confidential" number is that you indicated were -- these note-books were marked with.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, the one you're pointing to in this note-book 103 is "08/2-01-395." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who placed this number in this note-book, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I know. When I came to the unit, as I have already said, my job was to introduce some order, first of all. This note-book is the result of that effort. I'm sure that a full truck-full load of such note-books were burned down, because we did not have heating. This number was written by the person who kept records, and he would also put a number and a date when the note-book was registered. They would be shipped out to locations empty, blank, and they would be returned when they were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was each note-book that was used given one of these strictly confidential numbers?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Each note-book from the time when I arrived was registered, 99 per cent of them were registered. An odd one could have perhaps been omitted in this big workload, but every document was normally registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And aside from the collocutors and the frequencies that an intercept operator was required to put in the note-book, was it always the case that each intercept operator wrote down the date for a given intercept in the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: You can see on the note-book there is a date, the frequency, the time, the device used for recording. Here [indicates], it's "AR3000A." The speakers -- also, if we had an original document, we would have proper columns, and the speakers would have their own rubric or they would be designated as X/Y. But because we had to work very fast, there was a lot of work, we would sometimes omit one of these elements. Whoever works makes mistakes. That's normal. But the rule was to write down all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, thanks for that. We don't need that document anymore on the screen. Mr. President, I would like to tender 65 ter 869. Yes, I would like the Trial Chamber to be able to look at this original.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, you also mentioned just a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, you are tendering this collection of note-books as a photograph on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I also have a second photograph, but also of the note-book covers. If you'd like, I can show it to the witness, but it's basically the same. And I would also like to tender that as well. It's 65 ter 870.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P258.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, in your very last answer, your answer is recorded in the transcript as referring to an original document, and I just want to clarify what you meant by that because -- are you talking about an original document in the sense that it's printed -- a formal printed document, or are you talking about an original document in the sense that one that was originally transcribed or written into by the operators?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant we did not have original station log-books that were in use in the former JNA, properly formatted. We used this note-book -- these note-books in lieu of proper station log-books, and proper station log-books have columns already -- and boxes already printed out for all the various information that has to be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the note-book that I just showed you, the one that's written "103" on the cover, can you tell, from looking at it, whether that's an original note-book, that is, one that was created by the men in your unit, or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Absolutely, it's original.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, when these note-books were filled up, you indicated that they were -- that they were kept. Were they ever reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I oftentimes took note-books at random, whenever they were filled out, and compared them to typed reports. This was a system of checks and balances to avoid errors at the lowest level. I found them somewhat interesting, to be frank, because I would be reading these conversations and at the same time compare the note-book against the typed reports to make sure that there were no errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your review of these note-books, did you find any recurrent or systematic errors that were being made by the men in your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Well, naturally, there were typographical errors, a letter missing here and there, but there were no such mistakes as would impair the substance of what was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the tapes from which these transcriptions were made, can you tell us what happened to those? I know you've indicated previously that they were dubbed at some point and taken to other facilities, but, generally, what happened with those tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: In the process of checks and dubbing, the following would take place: If certain intercepts were recorded in a facility and a tape would be filled up, some four hours of conversation on average, then these tapes would be taken to the corps command, where the EDA department would play the tapes back, record important conversations onto a different tape, erase the contents of the original tapes, and return them to the facilities. So that was the procedure which was applied, for the simple reason that we were always in -- there was always a shortage of these tapes, we were always short of these tapes. It would have been normal for us to have a room full of tapes complete with all the conversations that had ever been recorded on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the information that was entered by the typist and then forwarded on to the headquarters, how was that -- was that information preserved?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: I think that it can all be found in the Central Archives in Sarajevo. The information is stored on CDs. Previously, they were called P-25s - they were somewhat larger diskettes - or 1.4-megabyte floppy discs. They are also stored in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would the information that's stored on those floppy disks and diskettes, would that encompass all of the information that is from the note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: All the information which was received by the 2nd Corps Command in the form of reports accurately reflected the content of the note-books. In the Counter-Electronic Activity Department, there was also a sort of checks carried out, where they would compare the reports which they also received against the audio-recordings. They would make sure that the recordings were accurately reflected in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive any information from that department or from that unit about any systemic or ongoing discrepancies between what's on the tape and the transcriptions that were created by the men in your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: There was a war on, and it was only natural that some mistakes were made, but the people from the department always asked that we gather as much information as possible. And this was our primary duty, to gather as much information as possible, regardless of the substance. So they always pushed us to do our work, to do more, and, of course, in that process errors are always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive a number of reports concerning errors, or instructions as to how to improve the performance of your men, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: During my term there, I didn't receive any such instructions. I said that there were negligible mistakes, typos, omissions to include time, but this was not deliberate. Still, we never received any set of instructions telling us how to address these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of the facilities with which you were attached, and I'll refer you specifically to the northern facility, were there other units operating from that facility? And if you need to name them, let us know so that we can go into a private session.

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: After I arrived at the northern facility, in one of the rooms there, there would be a representative or sometimes two representatives of the State Security Service, and they were the only individuals who were with us in the facility at the time. As far as I know, their task was to monitor, on the radio-relay communications of the Army of Yugoslavia or VRS, the conversations involving civilians, that's to say, political leaders. Their capabilities were modest. They had one or two devices; that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did they cover the same geographical area as the unit that you were attached to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Well, they were not able to cover anything else than the swath of territory we controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the 21st Division of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Yes. They, too, had a section. Their main duty was to cover the northern zone, i.e., Eastern Bosnian Corps, 1st Krajina Corps; in other words, the Posavina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that a unit entirely separate from your unit, or was it related to your unit in some way?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: At that point when I arrived there, the unit was independent. Its activity covered the area of responsibility of the then 21st Division or, in military terms, radio reconnaissance always covers up to 50 per cent more to the left and to the right. The information was sent to the intelligence organ of the 21st Division, their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did they at some point later on become affiliated or associated with your unit more directly?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: Toward the end of the war, that's to say, in early 1996, all these platoons, not just the ones from the 21st Division - there were others as well from the 22nd, the 24th, 25th - became part of my unit, men and the resources they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was information that you gathered and information gathered by the State Security and by the 21st Division, was that at some point shared amongst you in, say, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-032
utterances.text: In principle, very rarely; in principle, though. But as I've just said, depending on the urgency of the situation, if we received a piece of information which was very important and occurred in the area of responsibility of the 21st Division, it would only be logical that we forwarded the information immediately to these men, and they, in turn, to their units. This sort of information, which was of military nature, would be sent to the intelligence department of the corps and of the 21st Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could please have in e-court, it should be P239. And this should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I'm informed that this document, P239, is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not under seal. It was not tendered to be confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So it's just a question of whether it can be broadcast or not. All right, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it's not confidential, there's no reason not to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, then I think it could be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm sorry. Okay, it's okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on for the last minutes of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm showing you is an intercepted conversation. If we could go down to number 557. Well, I think we can see it fine on the screen. It's an intercepted conversation from the CSB. You can see at the top the caption is "CSB - SDB Tuzla," and it's number 557, and talks about a conversation between Ognjenovic and a general. And I'd now like to show you 65 ter 2923A. All right, this is a good place to stop, since I understand it's not on my list. So I'll work that out, and we can pick up tomorrow, with the leave of the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The only problem is we're not sitting tomorrow because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Monday, I'm sorry. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are running out of time. We are at the end of today's hearing. Mr. Vanderpuye, could you indicate how much time you will need on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I estimated about four for this witness. I think I can do it in less, but I'll have to hurry through a couple things to do that. I estimate about three and a half hours maybe, total. I think I've used two, so about an hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's just for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we have another issue which maybe we should -- well, we can raise, I think, in just a moment, in terms of scheduling for Monday. And I'm not sure, but I have to check with my colleagues to see, but I think we have a witness coming in on Monday who can only testify on Monday, and it may conflict with the continuation of the direct examination of this witness. So I'm sure it doesn't concern you so much, but we'll work out with our colleagues how to order it. But I think this witness's testimony may be interrupted as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should liaise with the Defence and find a good way to deal with the time of the Court and for the appropriate way to stay with the witnesses. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in touch with Mr. Vanderpuye and with Mr. Thayer, and I don't think that there will be any problem in interrupting the direct examination of this witness in order to accommodate the witness arriving on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, this witness will be heard on Tuesday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that we might be able to get him back on, on Monday, maybe after the other witness, but again I will talk to my colleagues and Mr. Gajic about that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I appreciate it. Thank you very much. Sir, we have to break now and to adjourn. I think your examination will be continued on Monday or on Tuesday. Mr. Tolimir will have some questions for you as well for a longer cross-examination. We have to adjourn now. When the Chamber has left the courtroom, then the Court Officer will assist you. And please be reminded that it is not appropriate to have contact about the content of your evidence during the break until Monday or Tuesday, no contact with the Prosecution. Thank you very much. Have a nice weekend, and we adjourn and resume on Monday.
